Do you believe that it is the job of the demographer or statistician to keep track of the percentage of matching once you deviate from the original key so as to give a statistical overview of how many matches were found using the first criteria, how many matches were found using the second criteria, how many matches were found from the third and so on and so forth." Her answer was: "Well, ideally we would like to have such statistics, absolutely. But if you think of how many millions of records had to be reviewed in this kind of procedures and how many matches first indicated as potential matches, then assessed, and then rejected, or partly accepted and so on and so on, it is a process that have been continued years and years long since the beginning of the Demographic Unit. So keeping these kind of statistics would eat up a lot of our time, if not all of it, you see, and there was also other work to be done in this period." And that ends Dr. Tabeau's answer. As a demographer, Professor, what do you say about her claim that -- as to why they could not keep statistics of matching when doing the work in the Demographic Unit.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Statistics of matching is very important for the simple reason that you can use it to assess the degree of combinatorics used in matching. Dr. Tabeau may be unintentionally mixing things up here. Correcting mistakes has nothing do with the statistics of matching. First, you correct the material to make matching possible because names are not correct, et cetera. In every process of matching I, and I believe all demographers and I know for a fact that statisticians do it when they work on official materials, they can keep statistics. What does that mean? First criterion, I managed to find so many matches. So, if after a while, some data has changed, I again say, I matched so many people on the first criteria. Why I don't agree with Dr. Tabeau, she is a co-author of that work, I suppose she has reviewed it. I suppose she knows that it's possible to draw the statistics of matching on the basis of what has already been matched. I'm not going into whether it was correctly matched or not. I think that these experts avoid statistics of matching because it reveals the degree of combinatorics that you used and that's why I find Dr. Tabeau's explanation surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say that Dr. Tabeau is a co-author of the work and you suppose she reviewed it. What part of this report leads you to believe that Dr. Tabeau had to know that they had statistics of matching?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know whether they have it, but it would be logical that they've made it without statistics of matching there's no point in working. You can keep matching one and the same material over and over again. When you have made a match, you remove it. When I've matched 3.000 persons or samples, for instance, I do not count them in the total number anymore. I go on matching with the rest. Whether they have it or not, I don't know, but from the very start, from the moment I saw the first report, I asked them to provide me with the criteria and the statistics of matching. I never got an answer on the statistics. I got an answer that has nothing do with matching. Namely, that they corrected thousands and thousands of data. Hundreds of thousands, Dr. Brunborg says for names and surnames. I'm not asking them how many names they have corrected. That's totally different. I'm asking them, after matching something with the first source, how many did you get in the first matching and how many did you get in the second matching. Dr. Tabeau is a co-author. I don't know whether she's read this or not. But when I sign something, I am careful about what I am signing. I suppose that if she is a co-author of this report, I suppose she's read it. There is a possibility but it's seems pretty incredible to me that Dr. Tabeau does not understand what statistics of matching means. Because from what you've just read out, she seems to be confusing things. The fact that they've corrected hundreds of thousands of something has nothing to do with this. That's not what I'm asking for. Statistics of matching is something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go back to the prior page in both versions to the top of this table that we looked at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you done with the statistics, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, this is a follow-up on the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, the data that is reflected on this table, can this be used to help the Office of the Prosecutor experts determine the statistics of matching that Dr. Tabeau said that they couldn't do?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know, it already existed, but it exists in the absolute amount. When you present it in the relative amount, it's much clearer. If you say that according to the first criterion, he matched 3.325 cases, if only it could be converted into percentages, 19 -- that would be 26 per cent. That is also statistics of matching. I can't believe that Dr. Tabeau does not consider that to be statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm about to move to a different point but if you have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What can you learn -- let's just assume that the statistics of matching were to be applied. What would it tell us? I mean, why would we be better able to understand or could it correct any inaccuracies in what is here presented as matchings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we had statistics of matching, we would be able to determine precisely what is acceptable as a piece of information and what is under a big question mark. You have a situation here where there are 45 criteria with modified or algorithmed years of birth. If Prosecution experts maintain that their sources of information are good, then they cannot claim at the same time that this degree of combinatorics is justified. If the experts had said, We'll take only three criteria, even then you would ask yourself whether a person who has an exact father's name, year of birth, place of birth could be found somewhere else and be a totally different person. It's possible, but it's highly improbable. But if you have the initial of the father, the initial of the surname, or maybe the whole surname with an algorithmed municipality and year of birth whether that person found in another list is really that same person, we can't know. The Prosecution expert says that, for instance, S. Radovanovic, born between 1945 and 1985, is probably me. No. The main source even though you use other sources is the main source. So I say, out of these 12 people called S. Radovanovic, born between these years, is probably this Svetlana Radovanovic. So there are no good quality sources of information that enable us to make a reliable matching. The main source is censuses. With the name and surname, it contains relatively the most reliable data: Name and surname, were never a datum in statistics, they were never processed. This is scanned material received by the Prosecution experts and that's why it features here and that's why it contains so many errors and that's why they made hundreds of thousands of corrections. The census was conducted in two scripts, Cyrillic and Roman; in different handwritings; pencils that are different. But I'm not going into the fact that they have corrected 100 thousands of names and surnames I can believe that they made good corrections. But if the numbers don't coincide, for instance, if the year of birth is not accurate, if you don't have an accurate place of birth, then how can I believe you that you've really checked that that Svetlana Radovanovic is indeed me. For instance, I can say I went to PHR or the Red Cross or the electoral lists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... isn't it true that you're going far beyond my question? What statistics could learn us. Because what you're telling us that you don't believe them. Would statistics have overcome that, your lack of belief in reliability of the accuracy of the sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not my lack of belief. I know for a fact, because I've looked for mistakes and I found mistakes. I know that these sources are not what we call good sources in statistics. What you before you, if we draw out these statistics, the first criterion is what a relatively good piece of information offers us. All the other criteria are questionable. We see that percentages that have been calculated show what degree of combinatorics they use to represent that something they claim is, indeed, what they claim it to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do they exactly claim on the basis of this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They claim with precision that with the census, their own list, not the one we're looking at but the one that contains 7600-something victims matched to 77 per cent -- 87 per cent. But they don't say out of which -- out of these 87 per cent we matched so many on this criterion, so many on that criterion, et cetera. I am not inclined to believe that these are relatively reliable data. And it's not even about belief. There is no belief in science. We need to show what is and isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm -- I'm misunderstanding it. But I see that at least that's how I understand this list, that if you match -- and, first of all, it is -- no, let me just see. I understand this list to be that comparing the information on that consolidated list, that if you take into account A, B, C and D there are so many matches. If you take into account C and D, it gives so many matches. If you take into account B, C, D, X and Y. I do not fully understand if you say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to explain. Precisely in order to conceal certain things, they represent this list which is a consolidated list of the Red Cross and PHR, not their own list as they show in the title. If they have shown matches of their own list featuring 7600 people, this dilemma would not exist. If they had provided matchings of the Red Cross, how could they not provide their own matchings? It's a completely identical process. I have a list of 7.600 names with different data, et cetera, I will put it through that procedure, and I will get so many matches. And intellectually what they are doing is very dishonest, they put one thing in the title and show something entirely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly in the title is it that is a lie? Is it the matching of the 2005 list OTP list with the 1991 population census? That what you had on your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There is a inconsistency between the main title which says matching the Prosecution list from 1995 -- from 2005 with the census of 1991. And now in the table it says an overview of the matchings of the consolidated list of missing persons of the Red Cross and Doctors for Human Rights, when we compare that, we get 19.000. His -- Brunborg's list is a consolidated list but it contains 7.000-something names. Now when I tell you consolidated list, you have to think for yourself whether it's a Red Cross list or it's consolidated with something else. There is no obstacle for me to release my own list which contains 7.000-something names and to match it with what I wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now ... yes, and you say that they're doing that to conceal something? What exactly are they concealing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether they wanted to conceal something, but I do say that with full responsibility that it's intellectually dishonest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just quote the beginning of your previous answer. "Precisely in order to conceal certain things they represent this list which is a consolidated list of the Red Cross," et cetera, et cetera. So when I ask you what are they concealing and if you are telling us that I don't know whether they wanted to conceal something, that was the beginning of your previous answer, that that was their intention. So therefore I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. I was trying to be nice. But the fact that you are not showing what you are supposed to show, that's something I interpret as concealing. Because you have all the prerequisites for showing it. You are not showing what you are supposed to show but what you think you need to show. But it's precisely this inconsistency between the title and the body that makes me think that they are concealing something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you say the fact that you are not showing what you're supposed to show, that's something you interpret as concealing. Where do we find what these experts were supposed to show other than what they said they showed? Where is it found that this is not what they should have shown but that they should have shown what you've said would have been better to show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the title of this chapter 2. Please look at the title because it says: List of the OTP. You although that the list of the OTP contains 7.000-plus names of victims. That's the OTP list. And you probably know from the Prosecution testimony how that list was formed. It was based on the ICRC and Doctors for Human Rights. So if you say matching the OTP list and then you give a title of -- for the table which says consolidated list of ICRC missing persons, according to the ICRC information, about 20.000 people went missing. PHR, according to Prosecution expert testimony, recorded about 6.000 persons that coincide with the ICRC list. So if it's a consolidated list of the OTP, it contains 20.000 names, because these 5 or 6.000 are already contained therein. It's not a Prosecution list. That's the information from which the Prosecution formed their own list.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can help, if you look at the text what they're comparing is 2000, whereas it is represented in the heading title that it's going to be compared to the 2005 list. So the combined list being shown to the reader of the document is not from 2005. It's from 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see in the text at least what looks as in -- inconsistency, but... okay. It's clear what your position is. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like now to return to the Table 6A that we looked at. That should be page 16 in English, page 18 of the Serbian of this report. And, Professor, you've already outlined for us that there are municipalities listed here that are actually in Serbia, such as Bajina Basta, Olovo, Loznica, Tara mountain, Valjevo, Ljubovija. What I want to do is focus right now on the total number of missing which includes those that are said to be from Serbian municipalities and we see 7.692. If we could turn to the very next page in this report and Table 6B and if we could zoom in on that, and now we have a table showing again 7.692 missing persons and this time it's place of disappearance, not by municipality, and by my observation, there are no places in Serbia that are identified on this table. Do you have a comment given between these two graphs about that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Locations are taken into account here as well. As I look at this, I believe that not a single one of these locations is from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could now -- let's turn to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, let me ask a question --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Ivetic referred to the number 7.692. Above that number, there's a number 312 and above that, bold numbers 7.380. Can you explain the number of 312.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, it cannot be seen here, but Dr. Brunborg in some of his previous reports said unknown locations, unrelated and so on, all of these are provided here without any explanation whatsoever. As you can see here, he says more than less, less -- more than 20, less than 20, those that contained more or less than 20 and irrespective of where they were. That is what I'm talking about, this superficial nature of this report that we just have to accept everything that the doctor says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was not part of my question. Is it possible that in the number of 312, all Serbian municipalities or locations were included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to all the documents that I had the opportunity to see, Dr. Brunborg mentions some locations that are in Serbia but have nothing to do with these towns. For instance, he found graves in Belgrade and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is not my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We saw first Table 6A and you claimed that there were many municipalities or locations which are in Serbia. Are these possibly included in the number of 312 people disappeared? That means from locations less than 20? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anything is possible. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go back to Table 6A, the previous page. Can you please look at this table again and tell me -- indicate the municipality in Serbia with the highest number of the so-called Srebrenica missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bajina Basta, and then it says seven persons went missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it therefore possible because it's less than 20 that this and the other locations in Serbia are included in the line total less than 20 in the next table, B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. Because if it says seven persons in Bajina Basta, why would there not be ten in Loznica, for instance, 15 in Valjevo? Why would those numbers be omitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go to Table 6B again? Next page. You say they are omitted. Is it possible that they are contained, that they are not omitted but contained in the line: Total less than 20, with the total number of 312 would not be to be considered as omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I disagree. If they don't have the names, they are definitely omitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But if Your Honour's question confuses the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Don't interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Don't interrupt Judge Fluegge. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so because I think that in any previous report that he wrote that contains these municipalities, he would have mentioned that in municipalities in Serbia he found such and such a number. And there's no mention of any such thing. If you look at all the previous reports according to locations, again, he says that he took into account those with more and those with less than 20, but he doesn't give the number for the municipalities as mentioned here. 320 is not a small number. I am deeply convinced that they were found in the municipalities of Serbia and that they went missing there so that Dr. Brunborg could write that. 320 is not a negligible number -- sorry, 312.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I received the answer I was asking for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll soon take a break, but you may already follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I didn't allow you to interrupt Judge Fluegge but if you wanted to say something which would assist us in answering these tables in the absence of the witness you have an opportunity to do so now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I think it's the witness answered in the last part of the question where she says I am deeply convinced that they were found in the municipalities of Serbia. And so the point is when a number is linked to Serbia instead of putting the place in Serbia, making it clear to the reader of the report that these are found in Serbia so that one could see how close or how far from Srebrenica they are lumped together in a category that says, "Total, less than 20," thereby hiding the fact that they're in Serbia not in Bosnia, which would be the focus or is the stated focus of the report. That's what I would have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was not what the witness said at the beginning of this line of questions. She said the locations were not included although --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And she's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Although the number, the total number, is exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I just wanted to find out if she has any explanation for the total number less than 20 so I received the answer she was able to provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And my only problem was that by saying locations were omitted in a language, in English even, locations omitted means the names are omitted. So they are omitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number of disappeared persons have been represented also in Table 6B, although as far as they are in Table 6A found to have disappeared in municipalities which are in Serbia, which all show a number lower than 20, they are put together in the Table 6B and it is particularly to us that necessarily, because all the Serbian locations are below 20, that not only considerable number but exactly a number which can be reconstructed on the basis of the first one, which is Serbian, which is not Serbian, to know exactly whether they were found within Bosnia-Herzegovina, or whether they have been found although in lower numbers in Serbia. Is that something --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Except we don't know what place in Serbia. We don't know the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't know that. I would agree with you. Looking at the fact that the total number is the same, that although we do not know the place that, at least the location as we find it in Table 6A seems to be - and again I would have to look exactly in the Chamber would have to look exactly as to how far these locations are away from Srebrenica whether they are all pretty close to it. But that's, of course, something to be further considered. We leave it by that at the time being. We take a break, and we resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn to page 14 in English, page 16 in the Serbian and look at Table 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Earlier, Professor, you had told us that the Prosecution experts had expanded the time to go even to 1996. I believe here is the table in the report that gives the information as to what percentage of victims on their list actually have dates of disappearance that are in the months after July of 1995 and even going into April of 1996. Did you have anything else you wanted to tell us in relation to the Prosecution experts and their use of time scope in relation to this part of the report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I'm trying so say that this is one of the cases that shows that they wished to get as many as victims as possible, I mean, really, that is not a significant figure, statistically. Of course, it is important when speaking of death as such, but then why this is being done, that something that I don't understand. When they provide a certain framework, they have to say I did this for such and such a reason and I did that for some other reason. If I'm not mistaken, the time for Srebrenica pertains to July. Again, as I've said, I can understand August as well. However, whether all of that went on until April 1996 that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at another part of this 2009 report, page 23 in the English and page 27 in the Serbian and we'll have before us Table 10. And well, on the English Table 10B is on the next page but let's see if we can work with what we have here. Now, Professor, in relation to these -- this table, in two parts, what would you wish to point out to us here that demonstrates a point of concern from this report of the Prosecution experts?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a table where the experts of the Prosecution are distributing data. Now they're reducing Srebrenica to these five municipalities and adding some other municipalities. Because, again, we don't know what the remaining municipalities are except for the point that what is included there, Serbia, I'm deeply convinced not. So now these are these 24 [as interpreted] cases so it's unclear. It is in sufficiently professional, say what is the remaining municipalities. Say what is Srebrenica and so on. Now something that is very interesting, the missing persons and dead persons, according to ethnicity from 1991, how could they obtain this ethnicity? By matching with the population census, and as far as we could see they did not use the questionnaires of the Red Cross and there is no reference to ethnicity there. However, what is less controversial is how they came to this ethnicity in the first place. The problem is that they claim there are 7.428 persons that are on their list of victims, and they claim that 87 per cent of these persons were matched with the population census and they distribute them according to these municipalities that they provided. They, themselves, say that they did not match 1.000-something persons I cannot see whether it is 1.013 or what it is. So they did not observe even their own methodology. Their methodology says the following. In order to prove that there aren't any fictitious persons on our list but that it's all about real persons, we matched this to the population census because the population census contains real persons who were alive in 1991, and we did not manage to match 1.000 such persons. So there are 1.000 persons that are unknown. They did not manage to manage this with a population census of a very high number. According to their methodology, whatever you do not manage to match is fictitious, does not exist. Now, how did the Prosecution experts describe the fact that they take into account something that they're own methodology says, no this is not necessary. How did they prove that these 1.000 persons are citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I can admit, because later on they include them in -- under Muslims. Because these are Bosniaks who fell victim. I can -- or, rather, the Prosecution experts proves that at least 1.000 persons from his list are not citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know whether they're Muslims. They may be Muslims. If they are not citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, how do they affect the situation and everything that happened in relation to Srebrenica? The expert was trying to calculate all of this and shows two variants - we'll see this later on - with and without these matches persons. Now this is what the point is here. They do not observe their own modified methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the clarity of the record there was one number which is probably incorrect the -- I think -- I don't refer to page it started with pages again. You said the following: So now these are the -- these 24 cases, so it's unclear. You were referring to remaining municipalities. In the table I see 124. Did you say 124?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said 124 or maybe I wasn't close enough to the microphone or something. 124 remaining municipalities, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now corrected on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could also correct if we could zoom in on the column that is under unknown and unknown on the B/C/S original, you had said at one point in time, 1.000, and I can't see whether it is -- I can't see whether it is 13 or just a little over 1.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does that assist in confirming the exact number for unknowns?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now focussing on those 1.001 persons which according to the Prosecution expert's methodology they could not imagine with the census, I'd like to look at 10B. And to do that, we have to go to the next page in the English and stay on the same page in the B/C/S. And if we could zoom in on the note below 10B, or on 10B itself, doesn't matter, we see that the figures for the municipalities have been adjusted by taking into account the unmatched records, the unknown, 1.001 for men, according to the original distribution of the matched records by their 1991 municipality of residence and ethnicity. Professor, what type of method or methodology is the author of this document using in distributing those 1.001 unknowns amongst the municipalities that are listed, despite not being able to match them to a person in the census?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The method of proportion. The method of proportion implies that you know a certain mass for which you have data and then you have a certain other mass, and you don't know what it is. Here we know a definite number of victims in Srebrenica, Bratunac, et cetera, and that's, let's say, 100 per cent, and then we calculate how many of the total number Srebrenica makes. Let's say 30 per cent. Now from this unknown mass, 1.001, we take away 30 per cent, that's 300-something and we place it in Srebrenica. Then we take Vlasenica, let's say it's 20 per cent of the total. We take away from the remaining mass 20 per cent and we place it in Vlasenica. That's the method of proportion, wherein you take the proportions in known relations and transfer them -- transpose them onto an unknown equation. That method has been abandoned a long time ago. According to UN recommendations, the method of projection is excluded, especially pertaining to age structure. And it's excluded precisely because that's a way to target certain numbers to get desired results. That's why it's excluded on UN recommendation. Every questionnaire has to be filled in and age cannot be not assessed by the method of proportion, and that has applied since 2000, and it applies to all the countries that conduct censuses in the classical way. That's why in the latest censuses you cannot find age unknown. In censuses of 1971, 1981, 1991, you can find age unknown, but then, again, only within the allowed margin of error, statistically speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your opinion what would have been the more proper approach to take as to those 1.001 unknown individuals that could not be matched to anyone in the census?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It cannot be matched. The experts show that it cannot be matched. If it cannot be matched, then how do they know that these people lived in 1991 in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Their methodology says if you haven't made a match, then you haven't proven that they lived in 1991. It would be professional on their part to exclude them. I'm not saying this because they should have to lower the number in that case, but at least they should explain. If they have 1.000 unmatched persons, where do they come from? How come there is 1.000 of them? Did I do the matching badly? Or were the sources bad? How come that the data is so poor that they could not be matched according to none of the criteria? At least an explanation should be provided as to why, from the first expert report to the last one, these persons still feature there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page in the Serbian and stay on the same page in the English, I'd like to look at the next table, Table number 11. What can you tell us about the manner in which the Prosecution experts have presented the breakdown of the population divided into age groups? Do you note any problems with this?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is absolute and conscious manipulation. It continues from the first report to the latest one. Why is it manipulation? We see here only relative numbers. You never see an absolute number. Relative numbers, according to a certain methodology, are obtained from absolute numbers. Please, pay attention to the heading, the first item that says: Population, age group, 1995, and then it goes in five years -- five-year intervals, concluding with 1990. How does the expert know which age group that is? In order to know that, he would have to know the total population in 1995 and out of that total mass of population for each municipality, they should find out the age structure. For instance, I have 300 persons aged between 10 and 14. I find a total number of victims from Srebrenica of X and 300 is 0.4 per cent of that. To do that - and he should get a Nobel prize if he managed to do that - he would have to calculate it with the methods that are normally practiced and that are very difficult to manipulate and an assessment is made on the basis of a certain known number. It would be the census of 1991 and censuses are usually used for that purpose. Then with that number from the census of 1991, they would have to add all those born in 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995 and then take into account all those who died in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995. The difference between the two are the population growth and then they would have to calculate which age groups account for how many. Then you have to know the migration trends and then you would have to say in 1992 so many people migrated out and so many people migrated into the municipality. They would then have to calculate the difference. First of all, there are no vital statistics about the number of those born in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995 in these municipalities, nor do we have a migration balance. But even without the migration balance assessments are never made based on population growth alone. Such data does not exist. Even if they did, the expert would have to tell us so many people were born in Srebrenica in 1992, so many people died in 1993, 1994, 1995. And then the age group is calculated starting from age zero. You add all the newborns, and every age group moves by one year because each of these categories applies to a certain moment. In 1995, in the category, let's say, between 40 and 49 years old, there are people aged 45, 46, 47, 48, and 49. In the previous year, it was not the same category because those who aged between 1994 and 1995 and turned 50 move into a different category. So without accurate data about births and deaths, it's absolutely impossible to create the age structure for 1995. Since the expert tells us that this is the age structure for 1995, it would have been nice if she could explain it but she doesn't explain it. Instead, on the previous page, she says that these numbers were based on the age structure in 1995, and here we come to the apples and oranges I mentioned. The person who was in the 40 to 49 category in 1991 is no longer there in 1995. It would have been nice if it were possible but it's not. That person has moved into the 50 to 54 age group. With the victims of Srebrenica, if they calculated how old they were in 1995 and related that to the number of population in 1995, those are apples and oranges. You cannot in 1995, when I am aged 50-something, you cannot look for me in the category in which I was in 1991. You cannot. So this is pure manipulation. And I'm deeply convinced that Dr. Brunborg and Dr. Tabeau know perfectly well that these calculations have absolutely no base in any methodology practiced anywhere and they even pretend that it's science. This table in this form including only relative numbers exists in all the previous reports. To this table in all the previous cases, I objected, and I asked: How did you get these numbers? The only change that was made was that here, the age was indicated in 1991 not in 1995. So the only correction is that in the title, they put age 1995, but on the previous page it still explained it's not 1995. Actually, it's 1991. The only difference is that these tables are now separated and they show those 1.000 persons who are not in Bosnia-Herzegovina and another table which does not include them. Even a layperson can understand that it's manipulation. If you look at another category, that is to say, the total, if you look at the total, you will see how obvious the manipulation is. Total implies that I have a certain mass of population. The total here should be the population for 1991, all the ages, from zero to 100 or from 10 upwards. We don't know which age they're using. And now from that total population, you derive the numbers for each municipality. And then the experts say in Srebrenica is 34 per cent, in Bratunac is 19.something in Vlasenica 11.something, in Zvornik 1.9 and in Han Pijesak 8.6. When you add up all these percentages, they do not make up 100 per cent. They come to 75 per cent. Where is the rest of the population? We don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do we have the 75 per cent? Let me just try to follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You add up 34.2 plus 19.4 plus 11.3, plus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... instead of giving numbers, could you tell us what exactly you are adding at this moment. What table? What column are you adding up at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Table 11. It says "total" at the end of the table. That total shows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the share. The share of victims in the total population. A total mass which is to us unknown. But in relative terms, it should be, it must be 100 per cent. If you add up the shares shown by the experts, 34, 11, et cetera, et cetera, that comes to 75 per cent or thereabouts. If that 75 per cent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... where again I do find that 34? Perhaps I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it's in the last line. Total --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to do the math now. There we are. If you add up all these numbers without the first column, it comes to 75.4 per cent. It's -- if it's total, it has to be 100 per cent regardless of which mass you are dealing with. The expert should have said, I'm only talking about population between 10 and 89. He could have taken the whole population from zero to 89. It's precisely because of the fact that he is transposing the calculations does he get these apples from oranges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if your calculation is correct. It's not. But it's not 1 00 per cent, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I get 89.6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You should not take into account 14.2 because that's the total for all municipalities. That's the ratio for all the municipalities in this total. You take only the municipalities Vlasenica, Zvornik, Bratunac, Srebrenica, et cetera. And the rest is the sum, the share of all these municipalities in the total by age group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the percentage in relation to the overall number of victims, or is it in relation to the number of victims as found in Srebrenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, Vlasenica, and Han Pijesak. Can you tell us which of the two it is because whether or not you end up 200 per cent, depends on what your total is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. These ratios should have been calculated from the number of victims on OTP lists, 7.000-something, broken down by municipality. And this indication of years, there should be absolute numbers according to age in 1995. Absolute numbers. So he had to know how much population there is in each municipality by age group. For instance, in Srebrenica, in 1995, there were 20.000 total population. 100 of them aged from zero to 10, et cetera. And then add up until you get 20.000. And then you say, I have victims aged 10 to 14. Five of them aged 10 to 14. 25 aged up to 19. And then in this absolute mass given for each municipality individually, you look for the share of a certain age group, and then you say -- This is interesting, for instance, the category 45 to 49. It says 10.4 per cent in Srebrenica. Out of the total men, 50.4 per cent were killed. In 1991, there were 808 men in Srebrenica of that age. In 1995, we have no idea. He had to show us this and he would have to tell us, again, we have 800 or we have 900 or we have 300 and then we would know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you've given us some thought for -- to think about overnight so that's perhaps further questions may follow tomorrow morning. Because we'll adjourn for the day. And Ms. Radovanovic, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. But before you leave, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak to anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have given already today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that is clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear to me. Thank you.
